title: The peninsula
hookLine: desert, oases, trade routes, and a people who prized poetry and hospitality
carry: a land of wells and words

cards: Sand ridges, for days. Then, low on the horizon, a smudge of green: date palms around a well.
A line of camels turns toward it, and everyone in the caravan already knows that well's name, who holds it, and what it costs to drink there. This is where the sirah starts.
Before a single verse came down, before the Prophet ﷺ was born, there was this land of distances, water and words.

teach.b: Arabic calls the place jazirat al-'arab, the island of the Arabs, since the word jazirah can mean island or peninsula. The Qur'an speaks to people who knew this land in their bodies.

When Ibrahim leaves his family near the House, his prayer in surah fourteen calls the place, in Pickthall's words, "an uncultivable valley near unto Thy holy House." No crops. Tradition places Mecca in that valley.
So how did people live there? Trade.

Surah one hundred six, named for the tribe of Quraysh, speaks of their caravans setting out in winter and in summer, and asks them to worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.
A desert town's living, in a few short lines. Not all the land was empty, though. There were oases, with wells and palm groves, and towns grew up around them.

teach.h: OASES, AND A TOWN CALLED YATHRIB.
teach.b: One of them the Qur'an calls Yathrib, the town later known as Medina. Along the routes between them, tradition remembers two things held in honor.
The first was hospitality. Where a traveler without water could die, taking in a guest was not a nicety. Stories are still told of Hatim of the tribe of Tayy, remembered as a byword for giving.
The second was words: poems memorized and recited at fairs and around fires. A good line could make a tribe proud.
A sharp one could wound. The Qur'an arrives in exactly this world. When it speaks of rain from the sky bringing dead land back to life, its first listeners knew what dead land looked like.
And when it challenged them to bring a surah like it, it was speaking to listeners who knew what language could do.

how: Mosque classes and sirah books often begin the Prophet's story with the land of Arabia before Islam: Mecca's dry valley, its trade, and the customs of hospitality and poetry the Qur'an's first listeners knew.

p: remembered as a byword for giving

s: Arabia before Islam was all empty desert
there were oases with wells and palms, and towns like Yathrib.
in surah fourteen, the valley of Ibrahim's prayer has no crops
Ibrahim calls it an uncultivable valley near the House.
surah one hundred six speaks of caravans in winter and summer
the journeys of Quraysh, and the Lord who fed them and made them safe.

games.q: you're traveling with a caravan, and at dusk a stranger stumbles in from the desert with no water. what did the custom of this land expect?
o: take him in and feed him.
sell him water at a fair price.
point him toward the next well.
games.why: tradition remembers hospitality as a point of honor here. where a traveler without water could die, taking in a guest was not a nicety.

practice: Close your eyes if you like and see a wide open land, sand or sea or snow, with no roads and no signal, and let the space grow a little with each breath out.
Notice what you would long for there: water, shade, a voice, another person, the things this land made precious.
If you pray, you can thank Allah for one of them you have today; if you don't, simply notice which one you'd miss first.
